RENAL__Foundations of Nephrology:
Overview — The Nephron & Its Segments
The nephron is the functional unit of the kidney (~1 million per kidney) — and renal physiology is fundamentally about what each segment does to the filtrate as it passes through.
The organising principle: the kidney works by filter everything, then selectively reabsorb what you want back — it filters ~180 L/day but excretes only ~1.5 L of urine, reclaiming the rest in a segment-by-segment sequence.
Why it matters: knowing which segment does what is the key that unlocks where diuretics act, how the counter-current mechanism works, where acid-base and electrolytes are handled, and why specific tubular diseases (RTA, Fanconi) cause their patterns — cross-ref glomerular filtration, tubular reabsorption, counter-current mechanism, acid-base, electrolytes, diuretics, RTA (all build on this map).
The Two Nephron Components — the spine
A nephron = a glomerulus (the filter) + a renal tubule (which processes the filtrate):
Component Role
Glomerulus + Bowman's capsuleFiltration — blood filtered into the tubule
Renal tubuleModification — reabsorption + secretion as filtrate flows through its segments
Two nephron types: cortical (85%, short loops) and juxtamedullary (15%, long loops dipping deep into the medulla — these create the concentration gradient for the counter-current mechanism).

Overview — Glomerular Filtration & GFR
The glomerulus is the kidney's filter — it produces the initial filtrate that the tubule then modifies; GFR (glomerular filtration rate) is the rate at which this happens, and the key measure of overall kidney function.
The organising principle: filtration is driven by pressure (Starling forces across the glomerular capillary) across a selectively permeable barrier, and GFR is tightly autoregulated by adjusting the afferent + efferent arterioles. GFR is the number that defines kidney function and CKD staging.
Why it matters: underpins eGFR/creatinine, CKD staging, AKI, the ACEi effect on GFR, and proteinuria — cross-ref the nephron (the filtrate's journey), BP regulation/RAAS, AKI, CKD, nephrotic/nephritic syndromes.
The Filtration Barrier — what gets filtered
Filtrate crosses three layers from blood → Bowman's space:
Layer Role
Capillary endothelium (fenestrated)Blocks blood cells
Basement membrane (negatively charged)The main size + charge barrier — blocks large/negatively-charged molecules (esp. albumin)
Podocytes (foot processes, slit diaphragms)Final filter; prevent protein loss
The selectivity principle: the barrier filters by size + charge → small molecules (water, ions, glucose, urea, creatinine) pass freely; large/negatively-charged molecules (albumin, cells) are held back.
The clinical link (high-yield): damage to the barrier → proteinuria:
  • Podocyte/charge-barrier damage → albumin leaks → nephrotic syndrome (cross-ref)
  • Inflammation → blood + protein leak → nephritic syndrome (cross-ref)
The Forces Driving Filtration — Starling forces in the glomerulus
Filtration is driven by the net filtration pressure — the balance of Starling forces across the glomerular capillary (same principle as systemic capillaries, cross-ref haemodynamics):
Force Direction Effect
Glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressurePushes OUT (into Bowman's)The main driving force for filtration
Bowman's capsule hydrostatic pressurePushes IN (opposes)Opposes filtration
Capillary oncotic pressure (plasma proteins)Pulls IN (opposes)Opposes filtration
Net filtration = the outward hydrostatic pressure exceeds the opposing forces → filtrate forms. The key driver is glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure — set by the balance of the afferent and efferent arterioles (next section); this is what's adjusted to control GFR.
Controlling GFR: The Two Arterioles — the core concept (high-yield)
GFR is controlled by the afferent (incoming) and efferent (outgoing) arterioles, which set the glomerular pressure:
Change Effect on glomerular pressure → GFR
Afferent constriction↓blood in → ↓pressure → ↓GFR
Afferent dilation↑blood in → ↑pressure → ↑GFR
Efferent constrictionBlood dammed up in glomerulus → ↑pressure → ↑GFR (maintains GFR)
Efferent dilation↓pressure → ↓GFR
The afferent/efferent logic: constricting the afferent drops GFR (less in); constricting the efferent raises glomerular pressure (more dammed up) → maintains GFR when renal flow is low.
The angiotensin II point (the highest-yield application): angiotensin II preferentially constricts the efferent arteriole → maintains glomerular pressure + GFR when renal perfusion is low (e.g. dehydration, renal artery stenosis, heart failure).
  • The ACEi/ARB effect: blocking angiotensin II → efferent dilates → ↓glomerular pressure → ↓GFR → a rise in creatinine (expected, usually tolerated up to ~30%); but in bilateral renal artery stenosis, GFR depends entirely on efferent constriction → ACEi → AKI (cross-ref).
Autoregulation — keeping GFR constant (high-yield)
The kidney autoregulates GFR to keep it stable despite changing blood pressure (over a wide MAP range, ~80–180 mmHg):
Mechanism How
Myogenic↑BP stretches the afferent arteriole → it constricts → maintains constant flow/GFR
Tubuloglomerular feedbackThe macula densa (JGA, cross-ref nephron) senses tubular Na⁺/flow → adjusts afferent tone + renin → regulates GFR
The purpose: protects the glomerulus from BP swings + keeps filtration constant; overwhelmed at extremes (severe hypotension → ↓GFR → pre-renal AKI; severe hypertension → glomerular damage).
Measuring GFR — the clinical number (high-yield)
  • GFR = the rate of filtrate formation (~120 mL/min normally) — the best overall measure of kidney function
  • Measured using a marker that is freely filtered but not reabsorbed/secreted:
    • Inulin = the gold standard (freely filtered, not handled by the tubule) — but impractical
    • Creatinine = the practical clinical marker → eGFR (estimated from serum creatinine + age/sex) → used for CKD staging (cross-ref)
Creatinine caveats (high-yield): creatinine depends on muscle mass (low in cachexia/elderly → overestimates GFR; high in muscular people) and is slightly secreted by the tubule (overestimates GFR a little); it also lags behind acute changes (unreliable in AKI, not at steady state).
Filtration fraction = GFR / renal plasma flow (~20% — the proportion of plasma filtered).

Overview — Tubular Reabsorption & Secretion
The glomerulus filters ~180 L/day indiscriminately; the tubule then reclaims what's useful (reabsorption) and adds what needs disposing of (secretion) → producing ~1.5 L of final urine.
The organising principle: the kidney's strategy is "filter everything, then selectively reabsorb" — most reabsorption is driven by the Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase creating a sodium gradient that everything else follows; secretion actively adds substances (drugs, K⁺, H⁺) into the tubule. Where each substance is handled was mapped in the nephron note.
Why it matters: explains glycosuria in diabetes, the SGLT2 inhibitors, how drugs are cleared, renal handling of K⁺/H⁺/urate, and transport-maximum diseases — cross-ref the nephron (the segment map), GFR (the filtrate source), glucose homeostasis, gout, acid-base, electrolytes.
The Two Processes — the spine
Process Direction Purpose
ReabsorptionTubule → bloodReclaim useful substances (water, Na⁺, glucose, amino acids, HCO₃⁻) — the bulk of tubular work
SecretionBlood → tubuleActively add substances for disposal (K⁺, H⁺, drugs, urate, creatinine)
The net equation: excreted = filtered − reabsorbed + secreted → the kidney fine-tunes excretion by adjusting reabsorption and secretion.
The Driving Force: The Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase — the engine (core concept)
The key principle: almost all tubular transport is powered, directly or indirectly, by the Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase on the basolateral membrane (the blood side):
  • It pumps Na⁺ out of the cell (into the blood) → keeps intracellular Na⁺ low → creates a gradient for Na⁺ to flow into the cell from the tubule
  • This Na⁺ gradient is then harnessed to drive everything else: glucose, amino acids, phosphate (cotransport with Na⁺), and indirectly water (osmosis)
The logic: the kidney "spends" ATP on the Na⁺/K⁺ pump, and the resulting Na⁺ gradient is the energy currency that drives reabsorption of nearly everything → so reabsorption follows sodium.
Reabsorption Mechanisms — how things get back into the blood
Mechanism Examples
Secondary active transport (Na⁺-coupled cotransport)Glucose (SGLT), amino acids, phosphate — ride in on the Na⁺ gradient
Active transportNa⁺/K⁺ ATPase (the pump itself)
Passive (down gradients)Water (osmosis, following Na⁺), urea, Cl⁻
ParacellularBetween cells (Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺ in the loop)
Water follows solute: water reabsorption is passive, following the osmotic gradient created by Na⁺ reabsorption (obligatory in PCT/descending loop; regulated by ADH in the collecting duct — cross-ref).
The segment recap (cross-ref nephron): PCT does the bulk (~65%), the loop sets up the gradient, the DCT + collecting duct do the fine, regulated adjustment.
Transport Maximum & the Glucose Example (high-yield)
  • Transport maximum (Tm): carrier-mediated reabsorption has a maximum capacity — once the carriers are saturated, the excess is excreted
The glucose example (the classic)
  • Normally all filtered glucose is reabsorbed (via SGLT2 in the PCT) → no glucose in urine
  • But if blood glucose is high enough that filtered glucose exceeds the transport maximum (the "renal threshold", ~10 mmol/L) → the carriers saturate → glucose spills into the urine = glycosuria
The clinical links (high-yield):
  • Diabetes: hyperglycaemia exceeds the renal threshold → glycosuria (+ osmotic diuresis → polyuria) — cross-ref diabetes
  • SGLT2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin): block glucose reabsorption → deliberately cause glycosuria → ↓blood glucose + osmotic/natriuretic benefits (diabetes, heart failure, CKD) — cross-ref
  • Pregnancy: lowered renal threshold → benign glycosuria

The drug-secretion point (high-yield): many drugs are cleared by active tubular secretion, and drugs can compete for the same transporters:
  • Probenecid blocks urate reabsorption (used in gout) and also blocks penicillin secretion (historically used to prolong penicillin levels)
  • The urate point: urate handling (reabsorption + secretion) → thiazides/low-dose aspirin reduce urate excretion → ↑urate → gout; high-dose aspirin/probenecid increase excretion — cross-ref gout

Overview — Counter-Current Mechanism & Urine Concentration
The kidney can produce urine more concentrated than blood (to conserve water) or more dilute (to excrete water) — and it does this using the counter-current mechanism of the loop of Henle to build a concentration gradient in the medulla.
The organising principle: the loop of Henle acts as a counter-current multiplier that makes the medulla progressively saltier from cortex to deep medulla; this standing gradient then lets the collecting duct (under ADH control) pull water out of the urine to concentrate it. The whole point is water conservation.
Why it matters: explains how ADH concentrates urine, diabetes insipidus, SIADH, why loop diuretics are so powerful, and the response to dehydration — cross-ref the nephron (loop segments), tubular reabsorption, ADH/water balance, BP regulation, diabetes insipidus/SIADH.
The Goal: Why Concentrate Urine — the rationale
  • The body must be able to vary urine concentration to maintain water balance:
    • Dehydrated → conserve water → produce small volumes of concentrated urine
    • Overhydrated → excrete water → produce large volumes of dilute urine
To make urine more concentrated than plasma, the kidney needs a hyperosmolar medulla to pull water out of the collecting duct → the counter-current mechanism builds that.
The Counter-Current Multiplier — the core mechanism
The loop of Henle has two limbs with opposite permeabilities, running in opposite directions (hence "counter-current"):
Limb Permeability What happens
Descending limbPermeable to water, NOT soluteWater leaves (into the salty medulla) → filtrate becomes concentrated as it descends
Thick ascending limbPermeable to solute (NKCC2 pumps out Na⁺/K⁺/Cl⁻), NOT waterSalt pumped out into the medulla → filtrate becomes dilute as it ascends; the salt makes the medulla salty
The "multiplier" logic (the key concept): the ascending limb actively pumps salt into the medullary interstitium → this makes the surrounding medulla salty → which draws water out of the descending limb → concentrating the filtrate there → which delivers even more salt to the ascending limb to pump out... → the counter-current arrangement multiplies a small gradient into a large one, building a steep osmotic gradient from cortex (isotonic, ~300) to deep medulla (very hypertonic, ~1200 mOsm).
The single most important point: the thick ascending limb pumping salt out (NKCC2) is what builds the medullary gradient — and loop diuretics (furosemide) block exactly this → abolish the gradient → can't concentrate urine → massive diuresis (why loops are the most powerful diuretics) — cross-ref nephron.
Urea Recycling & the Vasa Recta — the supporting players
  • Urea recycling: urea is reabsorbed from the collecting duct (ADH-stimulated) into the medulla → contributes to the medullary hyperosmolarity (adds to the gradient alongside salt)
  • The vasa recta (the medullary blood vessels): run in a counter-current loop alongside the nephron → this preserves the gradient (if blood flowed straight through, it would wash the salt away). The counter-current arrangement lets it supply the medulla with blood without dissipating the gradient
ADH & the Collecting Duct: Cashing In the Gradient (high-yield)
The medullary gradient is useless unless the collecting duct can use it to extract water — and that's controlled by ADH (antidiuretic hormone / vasopressin):
  • ADH present (dehydration): inserts aquaporins into the collecting duct → it becomes water-permeable → water flows out of the urine into the salty medulla → concentrated urine, water conserved
  • ADH absent (overhydration): collecting duct stays water-impermeable → water stays in the tubule → dilute urine, water excreted
ADH is the on/off switch: the loop builds the gradient (always), but ADH decides whether to use it → ADH = the regulator of final urine concentration.
ADH release is triggered by ↑plasma osmolality (osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus — the main trigger) and ↓blood volume/BP (cross-ref BP regulation); made in the hypothalamus, released from the posterior pituitary (cross-ref HP axes).

Overview — RAAS (Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone System)
RAAS is the body's main long-term regulator of blood volume, sodium, and blood pressure — and the kidney is both the sensor and a key effector.
The organising principle: the kidney detects a fall in perfusion/volume and releases renin, triggering a cascade that ends in angiotensin II + aldosterone — which act to retain sodium and water and raise BP. This note focuses on the renal mechanisms (how the kidney senses it, and angiotensin II/aldosterone's actions on the nephron); cross-ref BP regulation for the systemic cardiovascular picture.
Why it matters: underpins the ACEi/ARB/spironolactone drugs, renal artery stenosis, the ACEi-creatinine effect, oedema in heart failure/cirrhosis, and Conn's/secondary hyperaldosteronism — cross-ref BP regulation, GFR (efferent arteriole), the nephron, adrenal physiology, electrolyte handling.
The Trigger: How the Kidney Senses It — the JGA
RAAS begins in the juxtaglomerular apparatus (JGA) of the nephron (cross-ref nephron note) — the kidney's sensor:
Trigger for renin release Sensed by
↓Renal perfusion pressureJuxtaglomerular cells (baroreceptor-like, in the afferent arteriole)
↓Distal tubular Na⁺/Cl⁻ (low flow)Macula densa (cross-ref nephron)
↑Sympathetic activity (β1)Direct stimulation of JG cells
The logic: the kidney interprets low perfusion, low sodium delivery, or sympathetic drive as "low volume/BP" → releases renin to correct it. Renin is the rate-limiting step of the whole system.
The Cascade — brief recap
Renin → angiotensinogen (liver) → angiotensin I → (ACE, lungs) → angiotensin II → aldosterone (adrenal) — cross-ref BP regulation for the full cascade.
The two effectors that do the renal work: angiotensin II (fast, vascular + tubular) and aldosterone (slower, tubular).
Angiotensin II's Renal Actions — the high-yield renal detail
Angiotensin II raises BP and conserves sodium through several mechanisms, with two that are specifically renal and high-yield:

Efferent arteriole constriction (the renal one)Maintains glomerular pressure → preserves GFR when renal perfusion is low (cross-ref GFR)

The efferent arteriole point (the highest-yield renal application): angiotensin II preferentially constricts the efferent arteriole → maintains GFR when perfusion is low → ACEi/ARB block this → efferent dilates → ↓GFR → the expected rise in creatinine; in bilateral renal artery stenosis, GFR depends entirely on this → ACEi → AKI (cross-ref GFR — this is the renal RAAS exam point).
Aldosterone's Renal Action — the sodium/potassium effector
Aldosterone (adrenal zona glomerulosa, cross-ref adrenal note) acts on the collecting duct (cross-ref nephron):
  • ↑Na⁺ reabsorption (via ENaC) → water follows → ↑blood volume
  • ↑K⁺ secretion and ↑H⁺ secretion (the exchange) → so aldosterone retains Na⁺ but loses K⁺ and H⁺
The clinical pattern (high-yield): excess aldosterone (Conn's/primary hyperaldosteronism) → hypertension + hypokalaemia + metabolic alkalosis (Na⁺ retained, K⁺ + H⁺ lost); deficiency (Addison's) → hyponatraemia + hyperkalaemia (cross-ref adrenal, electrolytes).
Aldosterone is RAAS-driven (angiotensin II + K⁺), not ACTH — cross-ref adrenal (the key point that aldosterone is preserved in secondary adrenal insufficiency).
The Integrated Response — what RAAS achieves
  • ↓Volume/BP/renal perfusion → renin (JGA) → angiotensin II (vasoconstriction + efferent constriction + PCT Na⁺ + thirst/ADH) + aldosterone (collecting-duct Na⁺ retention) → ↑Na⁺ + water retention + ↑SVR → ↑blood volume + BP → restores perfusion → renin switches off (negative feedback)
The overall theme: RAAS = the body's "low volume" response → retain salt and water, raise BP.

Overview — ADH & Water Balance
The body must keep its water content (and therefore plasma osmolality/sodium concentration) tightly regulated — and ADH (antidiuretic hormone / vasopressin) is the master controller, adjusting how much water the kidney reabsorbs.
The organising principle: water balance is regulated separately from sodium/volume — it's controlled by osmolality (the concentration of the blood), sensed by hypothalamic osmoreceptors, with ADH as the effector and thirst as the behavioural partner. ADH decides whether the collecting duct keeps or excretes water.
Why it matters: explains hyper/hyponatraemia, diabetes insipidus, SIADH, the response to dehydration, and why osmolality (not volume) drives water handling — cross-ref counter-current mechanism (the gradient ADH exploits), the nephron (collecting duct), RAAS/BP regulation (volume vs water), hyponatraemia, DI/SIADH.
Water vs Sodium Balance — the crucial distinction (high-yield)
A key concept students often blur: water balance and sodium/volume balance are regulated separately, by different signals:

What's regulatedPlasma osmolality (= water content; reflected by sodium concentration)Extracellular volume (= total body sodium)

EffectorADH (+ thirst)RAAS/aldosterone (cross-ref)

The key idea: ADH controls water (concentration); aldosterone/RAAS controls sodium (volume) → this is why sodium concentration disorders (hypo/hypernatraemia) are usually water problems, not sodium problems.
ADH: Production and Trigger — the controller
  • ADH (vasopressin) is made in the hypothalamus, stored/released from the posterior pituitary (cross-ref HP axes)
Triggers for ADH release:
Trigger Sensitivity

↓Blood volume/BP (baroreceptors)A less sensitive trigger, but overrides osmolality when severe (e.g. major haemorrhage → ADH even if osmolality is low)
OthersNausea, pain, stress, drugs
The hierarchy point: osmolality is the normal day-to-day driver, but severe volume depletion overrides it (the body prioritises volume/BP over concentration when life-threatened).
ADH's Actions — what it does (high-yield)
The main action — water reabsorption (the "antidiuretic" effect)
  • ADH acts on the collecting duct → inserts aquaporin-2 water channels → makes it water-permeable → water flows out of the urine (down the medullary gradient built by the counter-current mechanism, cross-ref) → water reabsorbed → concentrated urine
  • No ADH → collecting duct stays impermeable → water excreted → dilute urine
The secondary action — vasoconstriction: at high concentrations, ADH (vasopressin) causes vasoconstriction → ↑BP (the "vasopressin" name; relevant in shock/vasopressin infusions).
ADH also drives urea recycling (contributing to the medullary gradient — cross-ref counter-current).
The Integrated Water-Balance Response — putting it together
Water-deprived/concentrated (↑osmolality)
  • Osmoreceptors fire → ↑ADH → collecting duct reabsorbs water → concentrated, low-volume urine + thirst (drink more) → osmolality falls back to normal
Water-loaded/dilute (↓osmolality)
  • Osmoreceptors quiet → ↓ADH → collecting duct impermeable → dilute, high-volume urine (excrete the excess water) → osmolality rises back to normal
Thirst is the behavioural partner — also driven by ↑osmolality (+ volume depletion, angiotensin II); together ADH + thirst keep osmolality remarkably constant.

Overview — Renal Acid-Base Regulation
The kidneys are the body's slow but definitive acid-base regulator — they're the only route to actually excrete fixed (non-volatile) acid and they control the bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻) side of the balance.
The organising principle: the lungs handle the fast, volatile CO₂ side (minutes); the kidneys handle the slow, metabolic side (hours–days) by reabsorbing filtered bicarbonate, generating new bicarbonate, and excreting H⁺. This note is the renal mechanism that your respiratory acid-base note referred to as "the renal arm".
Why it matters: explains metabolic compensation, renal tubular acidosis, the acidosis of CKD/renal failure, and how the kidney handles an acid load — cross-ref acid-base balance (the framework + 4 disorders), CO₂ transport (the chemistry), the nephron, RTA, CKD.
The Kidney's Two Acid-Base Jobs — the spine
The kidney does two things to maintain pH:
Job Where Purpose
1. Reabsorb filtered bicarbonateMostly PCT (~85%)Prevent loss of the body's main buffer (don't pee out HCO₃⁻)
2. Excrete H⁺ + generate new bicarbonateDistal tubule / collecting ductActually get rid of the daily fixed-acid load + replenish HCO₃⁻
The key distinction: reabsorbing filtered HCO₃⁻ just conserves what you have; generating new HCO₃⁻ (while excreting H⁺) is how the kidney replaces buffer lost in neutralising fixed acids — the definitive acid disposal.
Bicarbonate Reabsorption — the PCT (conserving buffer)
  • ~85% of filtered HCO₃⁻ is reclaimed in the proximal tubule (cross-ref nephron):
    • HCO₃⁻ can't cross the membrane directly → the cell secretes H⁺ into the tubule → combines with filtered HCO₃⁻ → CO₂ + H₂O (via carbonic anhydrase) → CO₂ diffuses into the cell → reforms HCO₃⁻ inside → reabsorbed into blood
The carbonic anhydrase link: this needs carbonic anhydrase → acetazolamide (carbonic anhydrase inhibitor) blocks it → HCO₃⁻ lost in urine → metabolic acidosis (cross-ref nephron diuretic map).
This is conservation, not new acid disposal — it stops bicarbonate being wasted.
H⁺ Excretion & New Bicarbonate Generation — the distal tubule (high-yield)
The body produces ~70 mmol of fixed (non-volatile) acid daily (from protein/metabolism) that the lungs can't remove → only the kidney can excrete it. It does so by secreting H⁺ in the distal tubule/collecting duct, buffered two ways:
Buffer system Mechanism
Titratable acid (phosphate)Secreted H⁺ binds urinary phosphate → excreted; generates new HCO₃⁻
Ammonia/ammonium (NH₃/NH₄⁺) — the major adjustable oneThe kidney makes ammonia (from glutamine) → it traps H⁺ as NH₄⁺ → excreted; generates new HCO₃⁻
The key concept: every H⁺ excreted (buffered as titratable acid or NH₄⁺) generates a new bicarbonate that's added to the blood → this is how the kidney replenishes buffer + disposes of fixed acid simultaneously.
The ammonia system is the adjustable one (high-yield): in chronic acidosis, the kidney ramps up ammonia production → can excrete much more acid → this is the main way the kidney increases acid excretion when needed (e.g. compensating for a metabolic acidosis).
Renal Compensation — the slow arm (high-yield)
The kidney compensates for respiratory acid-base disorders (and corrects metabolic ones) — slowly (days):
Primary disorder Renal compensation
Respiratory acidosis (↑CO₂, e.g. COPD)Kidney retains/generates HCO₃⁻ → raises HCO₃⁻ to buffer the acidosis (takes days)
Respiratory alkalosis (↓CO₂)Kidney excretes HCO₃⁻ → lowers HCO₃⁻
Metabolic acidosisKidney ↑H⁺ excretion + ↑ammonia (if the kidney is healthy)
The chronic-COPD point (ties to your framework note): chronic respiratory acidosis → the kidney has had time to retain bicarbonate → a raised HCO₃⁻ signals chronicity (the renal compensation has occurred) — cross-ref acid-base framework.
The speed contrast: lungs compensate in minutes (CO₂), kidneys in days (HCO₃⁻) → which is why renal compensation for a respiratory problem takes time to develop.

Type 1 (distal)Can't secrete H⁺ in the distal tubule → acidosis + alkaline urine; hypokalaemia, stones
Type 2 (proximal)Can't reabsorb HCO₃⁻ in the PCT → bicarbonate wasting (part of Fanconi); hypokalaemia

The RTA logic (cross-ref nephron/RTA): the type maps to where the acid-handling defect is — distal (type 1) = can't secrete H⁺, proximal (type 2) = can't reabsorb HCO₃⁻, type 4 = aldosterone problem (hyperkalaemic).

Overview — Renal Handling of Potassium, Sodium & Calcium
The kidney is the main long-term regulator of the body's electrolyte balance — fine-tuning sodium (volume), potassium, and calcium by adjusting reabsorption and secretion along the nephron.
The organising principle: each electrolyte is handled by specific transporters in specific segments (mapped in the nephron note), under hormonal control — aldosterone for Na⁺/K⁺, PTH/vitamin D for calcium. Where and how each is handled explains the dyselectrolytaemias and how the diuretics affect them.
Why it matters: underpins hyper/hypokalaemia, hyper/hyponatraemia, calcium disorders, and the electrolyte effects of diuretics, aldosterone, and PTH — cross-ref the nephron (segment/transporter map), ADH (water/sodium concentration), RAAS (aldosterone), calcium homeostasis (PTH/vitamin D), the electrolyte clinical notes.
Sodium Handling — the volume electrolyte
The principle: sodium is the main determinant of extracellular volume (where sodium goes, water follows) → so sodium handling = volume/BP control (distinct from water/concentration, which is ADH — cross-ref ADH note).
Where it's reabsorbed (cross-ref nephron — ~99% reclaimed):
Segment Transporter Proportion
PCTNa⁺ cotransporters (with glucose/amino acids)~65% (bulk)
Thick ascending limbNKCC2~25% (loop diuretic target)
DCTNCC~5% (thiazide target)

The control: aldosterone (RAAS, cross-ref) ↑Na⁺ reabsorption in the collecting duct; ANP/BNP promote Na⁺ excretion (cross-ref BP); the fine regulation happens distally.
The clinical logic: sodium concentration disorders (hypo/hypernatraemia) are usually water problems (ADH), while sodium total body content determines volume status (oedema = too much; dehydration = too little).
Potassium Handling — the dangerous one (high-yield)
Why potassium matters: K⁺ governs the resting membrane potential → derangements cause cardiac arrhythmias (the reason hyper/hypokalaemia are emergencies) — cross-ref cardiac AP/ECG.
Renal handling: K⁺ is filtered, largely reabsorbed proximally, then secreted in the collecting duct — and secretion is the regulated step that sets K⁺ balance:
Factor Effect on K⁺ secretion
Aldosterone↑K⁺ secretion (the main regulator — retains Na⁺, dumps K⁺)

The aldosterone link (high-yield): aldosterone retains Na⁺ and excretes K⁺ → so excess aldosterone (Conn's) → hypokalaemia; deficiency (Addison's) / K⁺-sparing diuretics → hyperkalaemia (cross-ref RAAS, adrenal).
The internal shift — the other half of K⁺ control (high-yield)
  • K⁺ also moves between cells and blood (not just renal):
  • Into cells (↓plasma K⁺): insulin, β-agonists, alkalosis → the basis of insulin-dextrose + salbutamol for hyperkalaemia (cross-ref glucose homeostasis, electrolytes)
  • Out of cells (↑plasma K⁺): acidosis, insulin deficiency (DKA), cell lysis (tumour lysis, rhabdomyolysis)
The diuretic effects: loop + thiazide diuretics → hypokalaemia (↑distal Na⁺ delivery → ↑K⁺ secretion); K⁺-sparing (spironolactone/amiloride) → hyperkalaemia (cross-ref nephron).
Calcium Handling — the PTH/vitamin D electrolyte
Renal calcium handling (cross-ref calcium homeostasis for the full picture):
Segment Calcium handling
PCT + thick ascending limbBulk passive reabsorption (follows Na⁺/water)
DCTRegulated, active reabsorption — PTH-controlled
The hormonal control: PTH ↑renal Ca²⁺ reabsorption (DCT) + ↑phosphate excretion + ↑vitamin D activation (1-α-hydroxylase — cross-ref calcium note); vitamin D also ↑Ca²⁺ reabsorption.
The diuretic-calcium link (high-yield — ties to the nephron note):
  • Loop diuretics block NKCC2 → ↓the gradient driving Ca²⁺ reabsorption → lose calcium (used in hypercalcaemia)
  • Thiazides → retain calcium (↑DCT Ca²⁺ reabsorption → ↓urinary Ca²⁺) → used to reduce calcium stones; can cause hypercalcaemia
The CKD link: failing kidney can't activate vitamin D (1-α-hydroxylase) + retains phosphate → CKD bone disease / secondary hyperparathyroidism (cross-ref calcium + CKD).
The Integrating Principle — how it all fits (high-yield)
The collecting duct is the fine-tuning hub: aldosterone drives the Na⁺-retain / K⁺-and-H⁺-dump exchange → which is why sodium, potassium, and acid-base handling are all linked there:
  • ↑Aldosterone (Conn's): ↑Na⁺ (HTN) + ↓K⁺ (hypokalaemia) + ↑H⁺ loss (alkalosis)
  • ↓Aldosterone (Addison's): ↓Na⁺ (hyponatraemia) + ↑K⁺ (hyperkalaemia) + acidosis
This single aldosterone-driven exchange links the three (Na⁺, K⁺, acid-base) — the conceptual glue of distal nephron handling.

  • CT angiography / MR angiography — define the stenosis.
  • Catheter angiography = gold standard (and allows intervention).
  • Bloods: U&Es (the ACEi-challenge creatinine rise), renal function.
  • Asymmetric kidney size (or bilateral small kidneys) may be a clue.
Management
Medical (first-line)
  • Cardiovascular risk reduction — antihypertensives, statin, antiplatelet.
  • ACEi/ARB can be used but with caution + close creatinine monitoring — avoid in bilateral RAS (the GFR drop hits both kidneys).
Revascularisation
  • Percutaneous angioplasty ± stenting.
  • Reserved for refractory HTN, deteriorating renal function, or recurrent flash pulmonary oedema.
  • Not routine — trials show limited benefit over medical therapy for stable disease.

Treat the underlying atherosclerotic burden.

Associated with nephrotic syndrome (esp. membranous — hypercoagulable). Flank pain, haematuria, ↓renal function. Treat with anticoagulation.

Cholesterol / Atheroembolism

After angiography / vascular surgery / anticoagulation. AKI + eosinophilia, livedo reticularis, blue toes. Supportive.

Thrombotic Microangiopathy

HUS / TTP — the microvascular renal vascular diseases (MAHA + thrombocytopenia + AKI). Cross-ref AKI / haematology.

Duplex → CT/MR angiography → catheter angiography (gold standard).

Overview — The Three Modalities

RRT = artificial replacement of kidney function when the kidneys can no longer sustain life — needed in end-stage CKD or refractory acute complications.

THE DECISIVE FORK = which modality: haemodialysis vs peritoneal dialysis vs transplant. Transplant is the definitive option; dialysis is the bridge to it, or the alternative for non-candidates.

Cross-ref: CKD (stage 5 = elective RRT), AKI (acute dialysis indications), hyperkalaemia / fluid overload (acute triggers).

When Is RRT Needed? (two routes in)
Elective (chronic): end-stage CKD — stage 5, eGFR <15 → planned dialysis or pre-emptive transplant.
Acute (emergency dialysis) — AEIOU

The guiding principle: transplant is the best option (survival + quality of life) where the patient is a candidate; dialysis sustains life while awaiting it or where transplant isn't possible.
Haemodialysis vs Peritoneal Dialysis — Advantages / Disadvantages
Haemodialysis
  • Pros: more efficient clearance; done by staff; dialysis-free days.
  • Cons: in-centre & travel 3×/week; needs vascular access; intradialytic hypotension; fluid/diet restriction between sessions.
Peritoneal Dialysis
  • Pros: home-based & independence; gentler / more continuous; fewer fluid/diet restrictions; preserves residual function.
  • Cons: daily self-care & good technique needed; peritonitis risk; membrane fails over years; dextrose load (hyperglycaemia / weight gain).
When RRT Isn't Appropriate — Conservative Management
RRT is not right for everyone. Frail / multimorbid patients (especially the elderly) may choose conservative kidney management — symptom control (anaemia, fluid, itch, nausea), dietary measures and advance care planning — which can offer comparable survival with better quality of life. High-quality supportive care is part of every CKD service.

Three modalities: haemodialysis, peritoneal dialysis, transplant — transplant is definitive.

Signature complications: HD = fistula problems; PD = peritonitis; transplant = rejection.
Overview

The commonest form of RRT: blood is pumped through an external dialyser (semipermeable membrane) that removes waste + fluid by diffusion / ultrafiltration, then returned.

Mechanics

Typically 3 sessions/week, 3–5 hours each, usually in-centre.

Access — the AV Fistula

A surgical arteriovenous (AV) fistula is the access of choice — created ~8 weeks before starting (it takes 6–8 weeks to mature). A tunnelled central line is the alternative when a fistula isn't ready.

ComplicationNote

InfectionAccess-site sepsis
Protect the fistula arm: no BP cuffs, venepuncture or cannulation in that limb.
Indications & Complications of the Session

Pulmonary oedema with AKI is a classic indication for urgent haemodialysis.

Intradialytic problems: hypotension (commonest), cramps, and dialysis disequilibrium syndrome — rapid urea clearance → cerebral oedema (headache, confusion, seizures); avoided by gentle initial dialysis.
⭐ Pearls
Commonest RRT; 3×/week, 3–5 h, in-centre.
AV fistula created 8 weeks ahead (matures in 6–8 weeks); tunnelled line if not ready.
Fistula complications: steal syndrome, thrombosis, stenosis, aneurysm, infection.
Pulmonary oedema + AKI → urgent haemodialysis; watch for disequilibrium syndrome.
Overview

Uses the patient's own peritoneum as the dialysis membrane — dialysate is run into the peritoneal cavity through a permanent catheter; a high dextrose concentration draws waste / fluid across by osmosis, then the fluid is drained.

Mechanics
  • CAPD (Continuous Ambulatory Peritoneal Dialysis) — the commonest form: ~2 L exchanges several times daily, done by the patient at home.
  • APD (Automated Peritoneal Dialysis) — a machine performs exchanges overnight, freeing up the day.
Who It Suits
Patients who are independent and self-caring at home.
Contraindicated in Crohn's / significant abdominal pathology (adhesions, prior surgery, stomas).
Key Complication — Bacterial Peritonitis
  • The signature complication; commonest organism = Staphylococcus epidermidis (skin contaminant via the catheter); Staph aureus is the other common organism.
  • Management: antibiotics added to the dialysis fluid — intraperitoneal vancomycin + ceftazidime (or vancomycin in the dialysate + oral ciprofloxacin).
Other complications: catheter exit-site infection, hernias, dialysate leak, membrane failure over time, and hyperglycaemia / weight gain from the dextrose load.
⭐ Pearls
Peritoneum = the membrane; dextrose gradient pulls waste across.
CAPD = commonest (~2 L exchanges/day, home, independent patients); APD runs overnight.
Contraindicated in Crohn's / abdominal pathology.

Overview
  • The definitive RRT — best survival + quality of life; native kidneys usually left in situ.
  • Surgical detail: graft placed in the iliac fossa, renal vessels anastomosed to the external iliac vessels; native kidneys NOT removed.
  • The spine of this note = the rejection timeline.
Donor Types
Living donor (best graft survival, can be pre-emptive) · DBD (donation after brainstem death) · DCD (donation after circulatory death). Matched by ABO blood group + HLA.

Memory hook: hyperacute = preformed antibodies (prevented by ABO/HLA cross-matching pre-transplant); acute = HLA mismatch (treatable); chronic = fibrosis (untreatable).

Standard regimen (three drug classes): a calcineurin inhibitor (tacrolimus / ciclosporin) + an antimetabolite (mycophenolate / azathioprine) + a corticosteroid (prednisolone). Induction agents (e.g. basiliximab) are used at transplant.

Demand far exceeds supply, so organ allocation is an ethical balancing act. The UK now uses an opt-out (“deemed consent”) system (families are still consulted). Ways to expand the donor pool: paired / pooled exchange and donor chains, ABO-incompatible and altruistic donation.

Overview

AKI = an acute drop in kidney function — a rise in creatinine and/or a fall in urine output over hours to days. Unlike CKD it is potentially reversible if the cause is caught early.

THE DECISIVE FORK: the cause sits in one of three places — pre-renal (before the kidney — perfusion) vs intrinsic / renal (in the kidney — parenchyma) vs post-renal (after the kidney — obstruction). This split governs the entire workup.

Cross-ref: intrinsic causes (ATN, AIN, rhabdomyolysis, HUS), CKD (the chronic counterpart), hyperkalaemia (the lethal complication), and obstructive uropathy / retention / stones (post-renal).

Overview

CKD = eGFR <60 (or markers of kidney damage — ACR ≥3, haematuria, structural or biopsy abnormality) for >3 months. It is the irreversible, progressive loss of nephron function.

THE SPINE OF THIS NOTE = staging + systemic complications. CKD is a slowly failing gland, and the downstream consequences are what gets managed and examined.
The decisive distinction at presentation — AKI or CKD?

Cross-ref: AKI (acute counterpart + acute-on-chronic), the cause subtabs (diabetic & hypertensive nephropathy), ADPKD (Inherited Kidney Disease), and dialysis / transplant (RRT for stage 5).

Causes
Commonest = diabetic nephropathy (the leading cause of CKD / ESRF), then hypertension.
  • ADPKD (autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease)
  • Glomerulonephritis
  • Nephrotoxics — NSAIDs, PPIs, lithium
  • Chronic obstruction; recurrent pyelonephritis
eGFR Staging

eGFR is estimated from creatinine, age, sex and ethnicity.

Staging also uses ACR (the G-stage + A-stage “heat map”): A1 <3, A2 3–30, A3 >30 mg/mmol. A low eGFR and high ACR together carry the worst prognosis — the ACR axis is what NICE uses for risk.
Falsely affected eGFR: pregnancy, high muscle mass, and eating red meat <12 h before the test.
Clinical Features

Often asymptomatic (found on bloods). When symptomatic: oedema, polyuria / nocturia, lethargy, pruritus (uraemia), anorexia, nausea, and hypertension.

The Four Major Complications
1 — Anaemia of CKD
  • Mechanism: ↓EPO production by failing kidneys → normochromic normocytic anaemia (typically once GFR <35).
  • Consequence: predisposes to LVH.
  • Management ladder: optimise iron first (oral → IV iron if target Hb 10–12 g/dL not met in 3 months) → erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (ESAs) — EPO, darbepoetin.
  • ESA side effects: accelerated HTN, bone aches, flu-like symptoms, rash / urticaria, pure red cell aplasia (anti-EPO antibodies), raised PCV → thrombosis, functional iron deficiency.
  • ESA failure causes: iron deficiency (commonest), inadequate dose, infection, aluminium toxicity.
2 — CKD-Mineral Bone Disease
  • Mechanism chain: ↓1-α-hydroxylation of vitamin D + phosphate retention → low calcium → secondary hyperparathyroidism → bone disease.
  • Tertiary hyperparathyroidism: after long-standing secondary disease the glands become autonomous → PTH stays high with a high calcium (may need parathyroidectomy).
  • Bone lesions: osteomalacia, osteosclerosis, osteoporosis, osteitis fibrosa cystica.
  • Management ladder: reduce dietary phosphate (1st) → phosphate binders (sevelamer) → activated vitamin D (alfacalcidol, calcitriol) → cinacalcet if hyperPTH persists.
3 — Proteinuria (drives referral + treatment)
  • ACR is the proteinuria marker — use a first-pass early-morning urine sample.
  • ACR 3–70 → repeat on a second early-morning sample to confirm; ACR >70 → no repeat needed.
  • Refer if: ACR >70 (unless diabetic); ACR >30 + persistent haematuria (no UTI); consider if ACR 3–29 + haematuria + declining GFR / CVD.
  • Treatment: ACE inhibitor (at ACR >30 with HTN, or >70 regardless) + SGLT2 inhibitor (added renoprotection).
4 — Cardiovascular Risk

CVD is the leading cause of death in CKD → statin for all CKD patients.

Don't forget the metabolic complications: metabolic acidosis (treat with oral sodium bicarbonate), hyperkalaemia (dietary K⁺ restriction; cross-ref acute management) and fluid overload (salt/fluid restriction, loop diuretics).
Management (slow progression + treat complications)
ACE inhibitor = 1st-line — renoprotective. A creatinine rise up to 30% (or eGFR fall up to 25%) is acceptable after starting; beyond that, stop and investigate for renal artery stenosis.
  • SGLT2 inhibitors — slow progression (esp. diabetic / proteinuric CKD).
  • BP control; statin for all (CVD prevention).
  • Treat the complications — anaemia, bone disease, proteinuria, acidosis, hyperkalaemia.
  • Avoid nephrotoxics (NSAIDs); dose-adjust renally excreted drugs; offer influenza + pneumococcal vaccination.
  • Stage 5 → renal replacement therapy (dialysis or transplant — cross-ref RRT).
Diuretics — mechanism: loop diuretics (furosemide) block the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter in the thick ascending limb (used for fluid overload, still work at low eGFR); thiazides block the Na-Cl cotransporter in the distal tubule (used for BP, but lose efficacy once eGFR <30).
Refer to nephrology if: eGFR <30 (stage 4–5); ACR ≥70; ACR ≥30 with haematuria; a sustained eGFR fall of ≥25% (+ stage change) or ≥15 mL/min/year; poorly controlled HTN on ≥4 agents; or a suspected genetic / rare cause.

Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis (FSGS)
  • Overview: a common cause of nephrotic syndrome in adults and a cause of CKD.
  • Aetiology: idiopathic; secondary — HIV, heroin, sickle cell, reflux nephropathy, Alport's, IgA nephropathy.
  • Biopsy: light microscopy = focal (some glomeruli) and segmental (part of each) sclerosis + hyalinosis; EM = foot-process effacement.
  • Management: steroids ± immunosuppressants; treat the secondary cause if present.
FSGS = the HIV / heroin / sickle-cell nephrotic; “focal + segmental” on LM; higher steroid-resistance & recurrence in transplants than minimal change.
Membranous Nephropathy
  • Overview: the commonest nephrotic syndrome in older (Caucasian) adults; nephrotic syndrome or isolated proteinuria.
  • Aetiology: idiopathic (anti-PLA2R antibodies); secondary — hepatitis B, malaria, malignancy (solid tumours — paraneoplastic), penicillamine / NSAIDs / gold, SLE, thyroiditis, RA.
  • Biopsy: EM = thickened BM + subepithelial electron-dense deposits → “spike and dome”; IF = granular IgG/C3.
  • Management: ACEi/ARB for all (reduce proteinuria); corticosteroids + cyclophosphamide (Ponticelli regimen) for progressive disease; anticoagulate if high VTE risk.
“Spike and dome” = membranous; anti-PLA2R; screen for malignancy / hep B in adults; highest VTE risk of the nephrotics; rule of thirds (⅓ remit, ⅓ stable, ⅓ progress).
IgA Nephropathy (Berger's Disease)
  • Overview: the commonest cause of glomerulonephritis worldwide.
  • Classic presentation: macroscopic haematuria 1–2 days after a URTI in a young person (the short interval is the discriminator); heavy proteinuria is rare.
  • Pathophysiology: mesangial deposition of IgA immune complexes.
  • Biopsy: mesangial IgA on immunofluorescence.
  • Management: isolated haematuria + normal eGFR + proteinuria <1 g/day → monitor; persistent proteinuria >0.5–1 g → ACE inhibitor; active disease / no ACEi response → corticosteroids.
Haematuria 1–2 days post-URTI = IgA nephropathy (vs post-strep at 1–2 weeks); mesangial IgA; HSP is its systemic form.
Post-Streptococcal Glomerulonephritis
  • Overview: nephritic syndrome 7–14 days after a group A strep infection (throat or skin); mostly children.
  • Pathophysiology: immune-complex deposition (IgG, IgM, C3).
  • Features: headache, malaise, macroscopic haematuria, proteinuria / oedema, oliguria, hypertension.
  • Investigations: urine dip positive for blood + protein; raised ASO titre; low C3; biopsy = endothelial / neutrophilic proliferation, EM subepithelial humps, IF starry sky.
  • Management: supportive (most children recover fully) — BP control, fluid / salt management, treat residual infection.
1–2 weeks post-strep (vs IgA's 1–2 days); low C3 + raised ASO; subepithelial humps + starry sky; good prognosis in children.
Anti-GBM Disease (Goodpasture's)
  • Overview: a small-vessel vasculitis causing the pulmonary-renal syndrome — pulmonary haemorrhage + rapidly progressive GN.
  • Pathophysiology: anti-GBM antibodies against type IV collagen (lung + kidney BM); bimodal age (20–30 and 60–70), commoner in men, HLA-DR2.
  • Features: haemoptysis (pulmonary haemorrhage) + nephritis (haematuria, proteinuria).
  • Investigations: renal biopsy = linear IgG along the basement membrane (hallmark); raised transfer factor (KCO) from alveolar blood.
  • Management: plasmapheresis (remove antibodies) + corticosteroids + cyclophosphamide.
Key differential — ANCA vasculitis: anti-GBM (Goodpasture's) vs ANCA (GPA/Wegener's). GPA adds upper-airway features (wheeze, saddle-nose deformity, sinusitis). ANCA subtypes: c-ANCA / PR3 = GPA; p-ANCA / MPO = microscopic polyangiitis.
Pulmonary haemorrhage + GN = anti-GBM; linear IgG; treat with plasmapheresis + steroids + cyclophosphamide.
Henoch-Schönlein Purpura (HSP)
  • Overview: an IgA-mediated small-vessel vasculitis, usually in children post-infection — the systemic cousin of IgA nephropathy.
  • Features (the tetrad): palpable purpuric rash (extensor surfaces of buttocks + legs/arms), abdominal pain, polyarthritis, IgA nephropathy (haematuria, renal failure).
  • Management: supportive (self-limiting) — analgesia for arthralgia; monitor BP + urinalysis for renal involvement.
Purpura (buttocks/legs) + abdo pain + arthritis + nephritis = HSP; IgA-mediated; the systemic form of IgA nephropathy; usually self-limiting.
Rapidly Progressive (Crescentic) GN
  • Overview: not one disease but a pattern — nephritic syndrome with rapid loss of renal function over days–weeks; a nephrological emergency.
  • Causes: anti-GBM (Goodpasture's), ANCA-associated (GPA / microscopic polyangiitis), severe post-strep / lupus nephritis.
  • Biopsy: crescents in the glomeruli (proliferating cells filling Bowman's space).
  • Management: aggressive immunosuppression — high-dose steroids + cyclophosphamide ± plasmapheresis.
Crescents = RPGN; think anti-GBM or ANCA; treat urgently (steroids + cyclophosphamide ± plasma exchange).

Overview — The Organising Principle

Each electrolyte has a high / low fork, and each disturbance is its own self-contained causes → effects → correction workup. The cross-cutting principle that organises the whole cluster:

ElectrolyteThe danger is…The watch-point
PotassiumCardiac (arrhythmia)ECG changes → act fast
CalciumCardiac + neuromuscularECG (QT) + excitability
SodiumThe brain (water shifts)Danger is correcting too fast

Cross-ref: AKI/CKD (commonest cause of hyperK), rhabdomyolysis / TLS (hyperK), hypercalcaemia (stones, RCC, myeloma), acid-base (K⁺ shifts with pH).

The Unifying Safety Rules
K⁺ and Ca²⁺ = potential cardiac emergencies → always do an ECG; treat urgently if severe or ECG changes.
Na⁺ = a water problem, not a salt problem → assess volume status first, and correct slowly (rapid correction kills brain tissue — in both directions).
⭐ Parent Pearls
Potassium & calcium → cardiac (ECG, act fast); sodium → brain (correct slowly).
Each electrolyte = a high/low fork with its own causes → effects → correction.
Commonest hyperK cause = AKI/CKD; commonest hyperCa = PHPT (outpatient) / malignancy (inpatient).
Hyperkalaemia

Causes — conditions: AKI, CKD, rhabdomyolysis, tumour lysis syndrome, adrenal insufficiency (Addison's), metabolic acidosis. Medications: spironolactone, ACEi/ARB, NSAIDs, K⁺ supplements.

ECG changes (the progression)

1Tall, tented T waves
2Loss of P waves
3Broad QRS
4Sinusoidal wave → VF / arrest
Treatment (if K⁺ >6.5 or ECG changes) — the 3-step ladder
StepDrugAction
1. Protect the heartIV calcium gluconateStabilises the cardiac membrane (doesn't lower K⁺)
2. Shift into cellsInsulin + dextrose (± salbutamol)Short-term ECF → ICF shift
3. RemoveCalcium resonium, loop diuretics, dialysisRemoves K⁺ from the body

Hypokalaemia
  • Symptoms: muscle weakness, hypotonia; precipitates digoxin toxicity (the key drug interaction).
  • ECG: U waves, small / absent T waves, prolonged PR, ST depression.
⭐ Pearls
HyperK: tall tented T → loss of P → broad QRS → sinusoidal.
HyperK >6.5: calcium gluconate (protect) → insulin-dextrose (shift) → resonium / dialysis (remove).
HypoK: U waves; precipitates digoxin toxicity.
Hyponatraemia (Na⁺ <135)

The decisive fork = volume status (you can't work up hyponatraemia without it):

Volume statusCauses
HypovolaemicD&V, diuretics, Addison's, salt-wasting
EuvolaemicSIADH, hypothyroidism, psychogenic polydipsia
HypervolaemicHeart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, renal failure
SIADH (the classic euvolaemic cause): inappropriate ADH → water retention. Causes = small cell lung cancer, CNS pathology, drugs (SSRIs, carbamazepine), infection (pneumonia). Diagnosis = low serum osmolality + inappropriately concentrated urine + euvolaemia; treat with fluid restriction (± tolvaptan if refractory).

Symptoms: nausea, headache, confusion, seizures, reduced consciousness (cerebral oedema) — severity tracks how fast it developed.

Treatment by volume status: hypovolaemic → IV 0.9% saline; euvolaemic (SIADH) → fluid restrict; hypervolaemic → fluid restrict + treat cause. Severe / seizures → cautious hypertonic (3%) saline.
THE CRITICAL RULE — correct slowly (<8–10 mmol/L per 24 h). Over-rapid correction of chronic hyponatraemia causes central pontine myelinolysis (osmotic demyelination) → irreversible damage. “From low to high, the pons will die.”
Hypernatraemia (Na⁺ >145)
  • Causes: usually water loss — dehydration, D&V, diabetes insipidus, osmotic diuresis.
  • Management: cautious fluid replacement (water orally / IV 5% dextrose or hypotonic saline); correct slowly here too (<10–12 mmol/L/24 h).
Rapid correction of hypernatraemia → cerebral oedema. “From high to low, the brain will blow.”
⭐ Pearls
Hyponatraemia → assess volume status first.
SIADH = euvolaemic, fluid-restrict (low serum osm, concentrated urine).
Over-rapid correction → central pontine myelinolysis (low to high, pons will die).
Hypernatraemia = water problem, correct slowly (high to low, brain will blow).
Hypercalcaemia
  • Causes (~90% from two): primary hyperparathyroidism (commonest in outpatients) and malignancy (commonest in inpatients — bony mets, PTHrP, myeloma); also calcium / vitamin D excess, sarcoidosis, thiazides, thyrotoxicosis.
  • Symptoms — “stones, bones, groans & psychiatric moans”: renal stones, bone pain, abdominal groans (constipation, nausea, pancreatitis), psychiatric moans (depression, confusion); plus polyuria / polydipsia.
  • ECG: shortened QT.
Management: IV fluids (0.9% saline) first-line; bisphosphonates for malignancy; treat the cause (calcitonin for rapid lowering, steroids for sarcoid / vitamin-D excess). Furosemide is no longer routinely recommended.

Cross-ref: renal calculi (calcium stones) and RCC (PTHrP paraneoplastic).

Hypocalcaemia
  • Causes: CKD (↓vitamin D), hypoparathyroidism (post-thyroidectomy), vitamin D deficiency, hypomagnesaemia, acute pancreatitis, rhabdomyolysis.
  • Symptoms — neuromuscular excitability: paraesthesia, tetany, cramps; Trousseau's sign (carpopedal spasm on BP-cuff inflation) and Chvostek's sign (facial twitch on tapping the facial nerve).
  • ECG: prolonged QT (arrhythmia risk).
Management: calcium replacement (oral, or IV calcium gluconate if severe / symptomatic) + treat the cause. Always correct magnesium — calcium won't rise while Mg²⁺ is low.
⭐ Pearls
HyperCa = “stones, bones, groans, moans” + short QT → fluids + bisphosphonates.
HypoCa = tetany + Trousseau / Chvostek + long QT → calcium replacement (correct Mg).
PTH + malignancy = 90% of hyperCa.
Overview

Four primary disorders — split metabolic vs respiratory, then acidosis vs alkalosis. The metabolic acidoses are further split by anion gap (the key diagnostic fork).

Anion gap = Na⁺ − (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻), normal ≈ 8–12 mmol/L. It asks: is the acidosis from added acid (raised gap) or lost bicarbonate (normal gap)?
Respiratory ↔ metabolic compensation: the two systems buffer each other. A metabolic acidosis drives respiratory compensation (Kussmaul breathing → ↓CO₂); a chronic respiratory acidosis (e.g. COPD) is buffered by renal bicarbonate retention. Compensation never fully corrects the pH — a normal pH with deranged CO₂/HCO₃ suggests a mixed picture.
Metabolic Acidosis (the anion-gap split)
Causes
Normal anion gap (hyperchloraemic)Diarrhoea, fistula, RTA, Addison's
Raised anion gapLactate (shock, hypoxia), DKA, alcohol, renal failure (urate), salicylate / methanol poisoning
Raised-gap mnemonic — MUDPILES: Methanol, Uraemia, DKA, Propylene glycol, Iron / Isoniazid, Lactate, Ethylene glycol, Salicylates.
Lactic acidosis (a raised-gap cause): Type A = tissue hypoperfusion / hypoxia (shock, sepsis, ischaemia, severe hypoxaemia); Type B = impaired metabolism (metformin, liver failure, alcohol, some malignancies, thiamine deficiency).

DisorderCauses
Metabolic alkalosisLoss of H⁺ or gain of bicarb: vomiting, diuretics, hypokalaemia, primary hyperaldosteronism, Cushing's, adrenal hyperplasia

Raised-anion-gap acidosis = MUDPILES (lactate, ketones, renal, toxins); normal-gap = diarrhoea / RTA / Addison's.
Salicylate poisoning causes both respiratory alkalosis (early) and raised-anion-gap metabolic acidosis (later) — the classic mixed picture.
Vomiting → metabolic alkalosis; COPD → respiratory acidosis; PE / anxiety → respiratory alkalosis.
RENAL__Kidney (cortex, medulla, collecti:
Overview — The Kidney & Its Nephron

The kidney filters plasma and finely tunes its composition, then delivers urine to the collecting system. Its functional unit is the nephron (~1 million per kidney), and its architecture is arranged to run the countercurrent mechanism that concentrates urine.

🔬 Image slot — kidney section at low power — outer granular cortex vs inner striated medulla with pyramids
Jobs of the kidney
Filtration of plasma at the glomerulus
Reabsorption & secretion along the tubules
Water/electrolyte & acid–base balance; BP control
Endocrine — erythropoietin, renin, activation of vitamin D (1α-hydroxylase)
Cortex vs Medulla — How to Read the Regions ⭐
🔬 Image slot — cortex (renal corpuscles + convoluted tubules) vs medulla (parallel straight tubules & vasa recta)
Cortex (outer, granular)
  • Contains the renal corpuscles (glomeruli) — the round structures that make it look granular
  • Convoluted tubules (PCT & DCT) — the cortical labyrinth
  • Medullary rays — bundles of straight tubules & collecting ducts projecting from the medulla up into the cortex (they lie within the cortex)
Medulla (inner, striated)
  • No glomeruli — parallel straight tubules (loops of Henle, collecting ducts) & vasa recta → striped look
  • Organised into renal pyramids; tips = papillae
  • Cortex dipping between pyramids = columns of Bertin
One-glance rule: glomeruli present → cortex; only parallel tubules & vessels → medulla.
Blood flow: kidneys take ~20–25% of cardiac output, but ~90% goes to the cortex; the medulla runs at low pO₂ while doing energy-hungry transport — the watershed that makes it prone to ATN & papillary necrosis.
Architecture & the Nephron
🔬 Image slot — nephron diagram — renal corpuscle, PCT, loop of Henle, DCT, collecting duct
Lobe vs lobule
  • Renal lobe = one pyramid + its overlying cortex
  • Renal lobule = a medullary ray + the surrounding cortical tissue that drains into it
Nephron parts
  • Renal corpuscle (glomerulus + Bowman’s capsule)
  • PCT → loop of Henle → DCT
  • → connecting tubule → collecting duct (not strictly part of the nephron)
Two nephron types
TypeCorpuscle locationLoop & role
Cortical (~85%)Outer cortexShort loops; general filtration/reabsorption
Juxtamedullary (~15%)Cortex near the medullaLong loops deep into medulla + vasa recta → urine concentration
Countercurrent: the loop of Henle is the countercurrent multiplier (building the ~300→1200 mOsm cortico-medullary gradient); the vasa recta are the countercurrent exchanger that preserves it (urea recycling adds to it).
Spotting PCT vs DCT in the Cortex
Proximal convoluted tubule
  • More numerous around each corpuscle
  • Deeply eosinophilic (many mitochondria), brush border, narrow/fuzzy lumen
  • Fewer nuclei per profile (cells are large)
Distal convoluted tubule
  • Paler, no brush border, wider & clearer lumen
  • More nuclei per profile (cells are smaller)
  • The thick ascending limb, returning to the corpuscle’s vascular pole, forms the macula densa just before the DCT
Full tubule detail is in the Tubules note — here just remember: PCT = pink, brush border, few nuclei; DCT = pale, clear lumen, more nuclei.
The Collecting System
🔬 Image slot — collecting duct with pale principal cells + darker intercalated cells; papilla / area cribrosa
1
Collecting ductsPale principal cells (ADH/aquaporins, Na/K) + darker intercalated cells (acid–base)
2
Papillary ducts of BelliniOpen on the papilla (area cribrosa)
3
Minor → major calycesLined by urothelium
4
Renal pelvis → ureterUrothelium + smooth muscle (peristalsis)
Collecting ducts have sharp cell borders and pale cytoplasm — distinct from tubules. The pelvicalyceal lining switches to urothelium (transitional epithelium), the start of the urinary drainage tract. Nephron (metanephric blastema) + collecting duct (ureteric bud) together form the uriniferous tubule.
Stains
  • H&E — regions, corpuscles, tubule types, collecting ducts.
  • PAS — highlights basement membranes (glomerular & tubular) and the PCT brush border (key in renal biopsy reporting).
  • Silver (Jones methenamine) — glomerular basement membrane & mesangium.
  • Masson trichrome — interstitial fibrosis (chronic kidney disease).
Clinical / Pathological Correlate — Where Disease Localises
Glomerular
Nephritic & nephrotic syndromes (cortex, renal corpuscle)
Tubular
Acute tubular necrosis (ischaemia/toxins) — commonest intrinsic AKI; muddy-brown granular casts; injures S3 PCT & medullary TAL; oliguric then polyuric recovery.
Interstitial
Acute interstitial nephritis (NSAIDs, PPIs, penicillins, allopurinol) → fever/rash/eosinophilia, WBC casts & eosinophiluria; chronic tubulointerstitial fibrosis.
Medullary
Papillary necrosis (diabetes, analgesics, sickle cell); medullary sponge kidney
Pelvicalyceal / drainage
Hydronephrosis, stones, urothelial carcinoma of pelvis/ureter (smoking, aromatic amines; painless haematuria, multifocal)
Cortical masses
Renal cell carcinoma (clear cell, PCT, VHL/3p; painless haematuria, renal-vein/IVC invasion, paraneoplastic EPO/PTHrP). ADPKD (PKD1/2; berry aneurysms, liver cysts).
Localising the lesion to a compartment — glomerulus, tubule, interstitium, vessels, or collecting system — is the framework for reading every renal biopsy.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Glomeruli = cortex only. Medulla has parallel straight tubules & vasa recta (striated look).
Medullary rays (straight tubules) sit in the cortex; columns of Bertin = cortical tissue between pyramids.
Nephron = renal corpuscle + PCT + loop of Henle + DCT; the collecting duct is separate.
Juxtamedullary nephrons (long loops + vasa recta) concentrate urine; cortical nephrons are the majority.
PCT = eosinophilic, brush border, few nuclei; DCT = pale, clear lumen, more nuclei.
Collecting duct = principal (ADH/aquaporin) + intercalated (acid–base) cells; sharp cell borders.
Calyces & pelvis are lined by urothelium → site of urothelial carcinoma.
Endocrine kidney: EPO, renin, 1α-hydroxylase (active vitamin D).
RENAL__Glomerulus & Filtration Barrier:
Overview — The Renal Corpuscle

The renal corpuscle is where blood is ultrafiltered. It is a glomerulus (a tuft of fenestrated capillaries) cupped by Bowman’s capsule. Together they filter ~180 L/day of plasma into the tubule.

🔬 Image slot — renal corpuscle — capillary tuft, Bowman’s space, vascular pole & urinary pole
Vascular pole
  • Afferent arteriole enters, efferent arteriole leaves
  • Site of the juxtaglomerular apparatus
Urinary pole
  • Bowman’s space drains into the PCT
  • Parietal (simple squamous) → PCT (brush border) epithelial switch
Two arterioles, not an artery-then-vein: a glomerulus sits between an afferent and an efferent arteriole — a high-pressure capillary bed tuned for filtration.
Filtration physics: net filtration pressure ≈ glomerular hydrostatic (~45–50) − Bowman hydrostatic (~10) − capillary oncotic (~25–30) ≈ +10 mmHg; GFR = Kf × NFP. Efferent constriction (angiotensin II) raises GFR; ACEi/ARB dilate the efferent arteriole (↓GFR, renoprotective); NSAIDs constrict the afferent (↓GFR).
How to Recognise It on a Slide ⭐
🔬 Image slot — renal corpuscle on H&E — glomerular tuft, clear Bowman space, flat parietal layer
  • A rounded tuft of capillaries with many nuclei, sitting in a clear Bowman’s space.
  • Outer boundary = parietal layer of Bowman’s capsule (simple squamous on a basement membrane).
  • Nuclei in the tuft belong to endothelial, mesangial and podocyte cells — hard to separate on H&E (need EM/IF).
  • Found only in the cortex.
You cannot reliably tell the three glomerular cell types apart on routine H&E — podocytes tend to sit at the periphery of loops, mesangial cells centrally; definitive work needs PAS, silver, immunofluorescence and EM.
Structure of the Corpuscle
ComponentDetail
Parietal layerSimple squamous epithelium forming the outer wall of Bowman’s capsule
Bowman’s (urinary) spaceReceives the ultrafiltrate; continuous with the PCT lumen
Visceral layerPodocytes wrapping the capillaries (the inner layer)
Glomerular capillariesFenestrated endothelium; high-pressure filtering bed
MesangiumMesangial cells + matrix — the supporting core between loops (intraglomerular); extraglomerular mesangium at the vascular pole
The Glomerular Filtration Barrier
🔬 Image slot — filtration barrier (EM) — fenestrated endothelium, GBM, podocyte foot processes with slit diaphragms

Filtrate crosses three layers that together give size and charge selectivity:

1
Fenestrated endotheliumPores ~70–100 nm (no diaphragm), coated by a negatively-charged glycocalyx → hold back blood cells & add a charge barrier
2
Glomerular basement membrane (GBM)Thick, fused; type IV collagen (α3/4/5) + laminin + heparan sulfate (negative charge) → contributes size & charge selectivity
3
Podocyte slit diaphragmFiltration slits bridged by nephrin/podocin → final size sieve
The three layers work together: the slit diaphragm is the major size barrier, the glycocalyx & GBM heparan sulfate the major charge barrier. Water & small solutes pass; cells and large/anionic proteins (albumin, ~66 kDa) are retained. Lose the charge barrier or damage podocytes → proteinuria.
Podocytes — the Visceral Epithelium
🔬 Image slot — podocyte (SEM) — cell body, primary processes and interdigitating foot processes (pedicels)
  • Large cells whose primary processes branch into foot processes (pedicels) that interdigitate over the capillary.
  • Between adjacent pedicels lie the filtration slits, bridged by the slit diaphragm (key proteins nephrin, podocin, CD2AP).
  • They coat the GBM with negatively charged glycocalyx (podocalyxin) and help make/maintain the GBM.
  • Terminally differentiated — poor at dividing, so podocyte loss is often irreversible.
Foot-process effacement (pedicels flatten/fuse) is the EM hallmark of podocyte injury → heavy (nephrotic-range) proteinuria — classically minimal change disease, where H&E looks normal.
Mesangial Cells
Structural support — anchor & hold the capillary loops together
Contractile — adjust capillary surface area → help regulate GFR
Phagocytic — clear trapped macromolecules & immune complexes from the GBM
Secretory — make mesangial matrix & cytokines; proliferate in disease
Mesangial expansion/proliferation is central to many glomerulonephritides: IgA nephropathy (mesangial IgA), diabetic nephropathy (nodular Kimmelstiel–Wilson), and lupus.
Stains & the Renal-Biopsy Toolkit
  • H&E — overall glomerular architecture & cellularity.
  • PAS — GBM, mesangial matrix & Bowman’s capsule (magenta) — assess thickening/expansion.
  • Silver (Jones methenamine) — GBM outline; shows “spikes” (membranous) & “tram-tracking”/double contours (MPGN).
  • Immunofluorescence — pattern of Ig/complement: granular (immune-complex, e.g. lupus/PSGN) vs linear (anti-GBM/Goodpasture).
  • Electron microscopy — essential for GBM thickness, deposit location (sub-epithelial/sub-endothelial/mesangial) & foot-process effacement.
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Minimal change disease
Nephrotic; normal light microscopy, foot-process effacement on EM; children, steroid-responsive
Membranous nephropathy
Common adult nephrotic; subepithelial deposits & GBM spikes; anti-PLA2R (primary) vs secondary (malignancy, HBV, SLE, drugs); highest VTE / renal-vein thrombosis risk.
Diabetic nephropathy
GBM thickening + mesangial Kimmelstiel–Wilson nodules; earliest marker microalbuminuria; ACEi/ARB slow progression.
IgA nephropathy
Commonest primary GN; mesangial IgA; haematuria 1–2 days after a URTI (synpharyngitic, vs PSGN’s 1–3 wk); HSP = systemic form.
Anti-GBM (Goodpasture)
Linear IF along the GBM; crescentic (rapidly progressive) GN + lung haemorrhage
Alport syndrome
Type IV collagen defect (mostly X-linked COL4A5) → split/basketweave GBM; haematuria, sensorineural deafness, eye signs
FSGS
Nephrotic; focal segmental sclerosis + effacement. Commonest primary adult nephrotic (esp. Black patients, APOL1); secondary to HIV/heroin/obesity/reflux; often steroid-resistant.
Post-streptococcal GN
Nephritic ~1–3 wk after strep; subepithelial “humps”, starry-sky granular IF, transient low C3; usually self-limiting in children.
ANCA / pauci-immune crescentic GN
Commonest crescentic/RPGN; pauci-immune (scant IF); c-ANCA/PR3 (GPA), p-ANCA/MPO (MPA/EGPA). RPGN triad: anti-GBM (linear), immune-complex (granular), pauci-immune (negative).
Two-syndrome framework: podocyte/GBM charge injury → nephrotic (heavy proteinuria); endothelial/mesangial inflammation → nephritic (haematuria, red-cell casts). Granular IF = immune complexes; linear IF = anti-GBM.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Filtration barrier = fenestrated endothelium → GBM → podocyte slit diaphragm (size + charge selective).
The charge barrier (GBM heparan sulfate + endothelial glycocalyx) repels albumin; the slit diaphragm is the main size sieve.
Slit diaphragm proteins = nephrin & podocin (mutations → congenital nephrotic syndrome).
Foot-process effacement on EM = podocyte injury = minimal change disease (normal on H&E).
Mesangial cells: support + contractile (GFR) + phagocytic + secretory; expand in IgA & diabetic nephropathy.
Glomerulus sits between afferent & efferent arterioles at the vascular pole; filtrate leaves at the urinary pole → PCT.
Silver spikes = membranous; tram-tracking = MPGN; Kimmelstiel–Wilson nodules = diabetes.
Granular IF = immune-complex GN; linear IF = anti-GBM (Goodpasture).
RENAL__Tubules (PCT, loop of Henle, DCT,:
Overview — Turning Filtrate into Urine

The tubule converts ~180 L/day of glomerular filtrate into ~1.5 L of urine by reabsorption (water, glucose, amino acids, ions) and secretion (H⁺, K⁺, drugs). Each segment has an epithelium matched to its transport job.

🔬 Image slot — nephron tubule segments — PCT, thin & thick loop of Henle, DCT, collecting duct
Rule of thumb: more transport work → more mitochondria → more eosinophilic, taller cells with basolateral infoldings. The PCT (biggest workload) is the pinkest; thin limbs (little active transport) are flattest.
How to Recognise Each Segment ⭐
🔬 Image slot — high-power cortex — eosinophilic brush-bordered PCT vs paler clear-lumen DCT
SegmentEpithelium & clues
PCTCuboidal, tall brush border, deeply eosinophilic, narrow/fuzzy lumen, indistinct cell borders, few nuclei/profile
Thin limbs of HenleSimple squamous (look like capillaries but no red cells)

DCTCuboidal, no brush border, wide clear lumen, more nuclei/profile, paler
Collecting ductPale cells with distinct (sharp) cell borders; cuboidal → columnar toward papilla
PCT vs DCT quick call: PCT is pink with a brush border & fuzzy lumen; DCT is pale with a clear lumen & more nuclei.
Proximal Convoluted Tubule (PCT)
  • Simple cuboidal cells with a dense apical brush border (microvilli), abundant mitochondria (→ eosinophilia), deep basolateral infoldings and lateral interdigitations (so borders look indistinct).
  • The workhorse: reabsorbs ~65–70% of filtered Na⁺ & water, all glucose (SGLT2 early S1/S2, SGLT1 late S3) and amino acids, most HCO₃⁻ (NHE3 + carbonic anhydrase), phosphate (PTH-regulated).
  • Secretes organic acids/bases & many drugs (e.g. penicillin, creatinine).
Generalised PCT transport failure = Fanconi syndrome (glucosuria, aminoaciduria, phosphaturia, bicarbonate wasting). Most vulnerable to ischaemia/toxins in ATN: the proximal straight tubule (S3) and medullary TAL in the hypoxic outer medulla.
Loop of Henle & the Countercurrent Multiplier
