Thin descendingSimple squamousWater-permeable (AQP1), solute-impermeable → filtrate concentrates
Thin ascendingSimple squamousSolute-permeable, water-impermeable (passive NaCl loss)
Thick ascending (TAL)Cuboidal, mito-richNKCC2 pumps out NaCl (water-impermeable = “diluting segment”); ROMK recycles K⁺ → lumen-positive voltage driving paracellular Ca²⁺/Mg²⁺ (claudin-16/19)
The TAL is the engine of the countercurrent multiplier: it pumps NaCl into the interstitium (water can’t follow), creating the hyperosmotic medulla that lets the collecting duct concentrate urine. Urea recycling (ADH-driven UT-A1/3 in the inner medulla) adds ~half the gradient; the vasa recta are the countercurrent exchanger that preserves it. Loop diuretics block NKCC2 here (→ hypercalciuria).
Distal Convoluted Tubule (DCT)
  • Simple cuboidal, no brush border, a wide clear lumen and more nuclei per profile than the PCT.
  • Reabsorbs Na⁺/Cl⁻ via the NCC cotransporter (the thiazide target); Ca²⁺ via TRPV5 (PTH-stimulated) and Mg²⁺ via TRPM6 (hence DCT/Gitelman → hypomagnesaemia).
  • The end of the TAL, at the TAL–DCT transition, abuts the parent corpuscle as the macula densa (JGA — senses tubular NaCl).
Loss-of-function of the DCT NCC mimics chronic thiazide use = Gitelman syndrome (hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, hypocalciuria).
Collecting Duct — Final Tuning
🔬 Image slot — collecting duct — pale principal cells and darker intercalated cells with distinct borders
Principal cells
  • ADH → V2 receptor → cAMP → aquaporin-2 insertion → water reabsorption (V2 = vaptan/lithium target)
  • ENaC Na⁺ reabsorption & ROMK K⁺ secretion (flow-dependent), both up-regulated by aldosterone
Intercalated cells
  • α-intercalated: secrete H⁺ (acid) — reabsorb HCO₃⁻
  • β-intercalated: secrete HCO₃⁻ — the acid–base fine-tuners
Without ADH (central DI) or with AQP2/V2 defects (nephrogenic DI) → dilute urine. Acquired nephrogenic DI: lithium, hypercalcaemia, hypokalaemia. Its mirror is SIADH (excess ADH → concentrated urine, dilutional hyponatraemia; treat with fluid restriction / vaptans).
Transporter & Diuretic Map (High-Yield)
SegmentTransporterDrug that acts here
PCTCarbonic anhydrase (HCO₃⁻)Acetazolamide; mannitol (osmotic)
Thick ascending limbNKCC2Loop diuretics (furosemide)
DCTNCCThiazides
Collecting ductENaC / aldosterone receptorAmiloride (ENaC); spironolactone (aldosterone)
Collecting ductV2 receptor (ADH/AQP2)Vaptans (tolvaptan) — SIADH/ADPKD
Match the inherited tubulopathy to the diuretic that mimics it: Bartter = TAL/NKCC2 (loop), Gitelman = DCT/NCC (thiazide), Liddle = ENaC gain (opposite of amiloride).
Stains
  • H&E — segment recognition by cell height, brush border, lumen & nuclei.
  • PAS — accentuates the PCT brush border & tubular basement membranes.
  • In ATN, look for muddy-brown granular casts and loss/sloughing of the brush border.
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Acute tubular necrosis
PCT & TAL injury (ischaemia/toxins) → muddy-brown casts; commonest intrinsic AKI
Fanconi syndrome
Generalised PCT failure → glucosuria, aminoaciduria, phosphaturia, proximal RTA
Bartter syndrome
TAL / NKCC2 defect (loop-diuretic-like); hypokalaemic alkalosis, hypercalciuria
Gitelman syndrome
DCT / NCC defect (thiazide-like); hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, hypocalciuria
Liddle syndrome
ENaC gain of function → Na⁺ retention, hypertension, hypokalaemia (aldosterone low)
Diabetes insipidus / RTA
ADH–AQP2 failure → dilute urine (DI). RTA: type 1 distal (α-intercalated H⁺), type 2 proximal (Fanconi) — both hypokalaemic; type 4 hypoaldosteronism — hyperkalaemic.
⭐ Exam Pearls
PCT = brush border, eosinophilic, fuzzy lumen, few nuclei; reabsorbs 65–70% + all glucose/amino acids.
Thin limbs = squamous (like capillaries, no RBCs); descending = water out, ascending = salt out.
TAL = the diluting segment; NKCC2 builds the medullary gradient; blocked by loop diuretics.
DCT = pale, clear lumen, more nuclei; NCC (thiazide target); Ca²⁺ reabsorption under PTH.
Collecting duct = principal cells (ADH/AQP2, ENaC, aldosterone) + intercalated cells (acid–base).
Diuretic map: acetazolamide-PCT, loop-TAL, thiazide-DCT, amiloride/spironolactone-CD.
Tubulopathies: Bartter = loop-like, Gitelman = thiazide-like, Liddle = ENaC gain.
ATN hits the PCT & TAL → muddy-brown granular casts; Fanconi = global PCT failure.
RENAL__Juxtaglomerular Apparatus:
Overview — The Kidney’s Control Centre

The juxtaglomerular apparatus (JGA) sits at the vascular pole, where a nephron’s own distal tubule (macula densa) touches its afferent & efferent arterioles. It is the sensor–effector unit for blood pressure/volume (renin) and for GFR autoregulation (tubuloglomerular feedback).

🔬 Image slot — juxtaglomerular apparatus at the vascular pole — macula densa, JG cells, extraglomerular mesangium
Elegant feedback loop: the distal tubule loops back to its own glomerulus so the nephron can report its salt delivery and adjust its own filtration and renin output.
How to Recognise It on a Slide ⭐
🔬 Image slot — macula densa — a patch of tall, crowded distal-tubule nuclei against the vascular pole
  • Macula densa — a focal patch of tall, narrow, crowded nuclei at the end of the thick ascending limb where it hugs the vascular pole (the “dense spot”).
  • JG (granular) cells — plump cells in the afferent arteriole wall with pale/granular cytoplasm (PAS-positive renin granules).
  • Extraglomerular mesangium — pale cells filling the triangle between the two arterioles and the macula densa.
Find the vascular pole, then look for the crowded macula-densa nuclei opposite the granular-walled afferent arteriole — that triangle is the JGA.
The Three Components
ComponentOriginRole
Macula densaEnd of the thick ascending limb (TAL–DCT junction)Chemosensor of luminal Cl⁻ via apical NKCC2 (the loop-diuretic target)
Juxtaglomerular (granular) cellsModified smooth muscle of the afferent arterioleSecrete renin; also act as an intrarenal baroreceptor
Extraglomerular mesangial (lacis / Goormaghtigh) cellsMesangial lineageBridge the macula densa & arterioles; relay signals (gap junctions)
Renin Release & the RAAS
🔬 Image slot — renin-angiotensin-aldosterone pathway from JG-cell renin to angiotensin II effects
Three triggers for renin release
↓ Renal perfusion pressure sensed by the afferent-arteriole baroreceptor
↓ NaCl at the macula densa (low distal delivery)
Sympathetic β₁ stimulation of JG cells
The cascade
1
ReninJG cells cleave angiotensinogen (liver) → angiotensin I
2
ACELung endothelium: angiotensin I → angiotensin II
3
Angiotensin II effectsVia AT1: vasoconstriction, aldosterone, ADH, thirst, ↑ proximal Na⁺, sympathetic facilitation & cardiac/vascular remodelling
4
↑ BP & volumeRestores perfusion; ANG II also directly suppresses JG renin (short-loop AT1 feedback)
Angiotensin II preferentially constricts the EFFERENT arteriole → keeps glomerular pressure & GFR up when perfusion falls — the reason ACE inhibitors/ARBs can drop GFR (and are risky in bilateral renal artery stenosis).
ACE = kininase II: it also degrades bradykinin, so ACE inhibitors raise bradykinin → dry cough (~10–20%) & angioedema. ARBs block the AT1 receptor directly, don’t raise bradykinin, so cause less cough — the usual switch when ACEi cough develops.
Tubuloglomerular Feedback (GFR Autoregulation)
🔬 Image slot — tubuloglomerular feedback loop — macula densa NaCl sensing to afferent arteriolar tone
GFR too HIGH
  • ↑ NaCl reaches the macula densa
  • → releases adenosine → afferent constriction
  • → ↓ GFR back to normal (and ↓ renin)
GFR too LOW
  • ↓ NaCl at the macula densa
  • → afferent dilation (prostaglandins) + ↑ renin
  • → ↑ GFR restored
This intrarenal loop plus the faster myogenic response (afferent stretch → constriction) keep GFR & renal blood flow stable across MAP ≈ 80–180 mmHg (autoregulation). The macula densa signals via ATP→adenosine (A1 receptors) to constrict, and via COX-2 → PGE₂ to stimulate renin when NaCl is low.
Arteriolar Tone & GFR — the Drug Angle
  • Afferent dilation / efferent constriction both raise glomerular pressure & GFR.
  • Prostaglandins dilate the afferent arteriole → NSAIDs (which block them) can drop GFR, especially in volume depletion.
  • Angiotensin II constricts the efferent arteriole → ACE inhibitors/ARBs dilate it, lowering intraglomerular pressure (renoprotective in proteinuria, but ↓ GFR acutely).
A-fferent = NSAIDs; E-fferent = ACE inhibitors. A handy memory hook for which drug hits which arteriole.
Stains
  • H&E — crowded macula-densa nuclei; granular JG cells in the afferent wall.
  • PAS — JG-cell renin granules (magenta) & the arteriolar/tubular basement membranes.
  • Immunohistochemistry for renin — confirms JG cells (and reninomas).
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Renovascular hypertension
Renal artery stenosis → ↓ perfusion → ↑ renin → secondary hypertension
Reninoma (JG-cell tumour)
Rare renin-secreting tumour → hypertension + hypokalaemia + high renin & aldosterone
RAAS-blocking drugs
ACE inhibitors, ARBs, aliskiren (renin), spironolactone (aldosterone); β-blockers ↓ renin
Bilateral renal artery stenosis
GFR is angiotensin-II (efferent) dependent → ACEi/ARB can precipitate AKI
NSAID nephrotoxicity
Block afferent-dilating prostaglandins → ↓ GFR (risk in hypovolaemia/CKD)
Heart failure / hypovolaemia
RAAS over-activation drives Na/water retention (target of ACEi + aldosterone antagonists)
SGLT2 inhibitors & TGF
Block proximal Na/glucose → more NaCl at the macula densa → TGF afferent constriction → lowers hyperfiltration — renoprotective in diabetic/CKD.
Aldosterone:renin ratio (ARR)
Conn’s: high aldosterone, low renin → high ARR. Renovascular / reninoma: both high → low/normal ARR — the key discriminator.
⭐ Exam Pearls
JGA = macula densa (distal tubule NaCl sensor) + JG granular cells (renin, afferent baroreceptor) + extraglomerular mesangium.
Three renin triggers: ↓ perfusion (baroreceptor), ↓ macula-densa NaCl, sympathetic β₁.
RAAS: renin → ANG I → (ACE, lung) → ANG II → vasoconstriction + aldosterone + ADH + thirst → ↑ BP/volume.
ANG II constricts the efferent arteriole to preserve GFR — hence ACEi/ARB caution in bilateral RAS.
Tubuloglomerular feedback: ↑ macula-densa NaCl → adenosine → afferent constriction → ↓ GFR (autoregulation).
A-fferent = NSAIDs (prostaglandins); E-fferent = ACE inhibitors (angiotensin II).
Macula densa = tall crowded nuclei in the distal tubule at the vascular pole.
Renin-secreting tumour (reninoma) → hypertension + hypokalaemia with high renin.
RENAL__Ureter & Bladder:
Overview — The Urinary Drainage & Storage Tract

Beyond the collecting ducts, urine passes through a conducting & storage tract: calyces → renal pelvis → ureter → bladder → urethra. It is lined throughout by urothelium (transitional epithelium) — a distensible, waterproof barrier — wrapped in smooth muscle for peristalsis and voiding.

🔬 Image slot — urinary tract overview — pelvis, ureter, bladder, urethra all lined by urothelium
Two jobs, one epithelium: the urothelium must stretch enormously (empty → full bladder) yet stay impermeable so hypertonic/toxic urine cannot leak back into the blood.
Urothelium — How to Recognise It ⭐
🔬 Image slot — urothelium — dome-shaped umbrella cells over intermediate & basal layers (relaxed vs distended)
  • Umbrella (superficial) cells — large, dome-shaped, often binucleate, bulging into the lumen; the diagnostic top layer.
  • Intermediate cells (several layers) + a single basal cell layer on the basement membrane.
  • Distension-dependent look: relaxed → rounded cells, ~5–6 apparent layers; distended → flat cells, only 2–3 apparent layers.
  • Umbrella cells have an asymmetric unit membrane with uroplakin plaques + fusiform (discoidal) vesicles that unfold to add surface area, tight junctions, and an apical glycosaminoglycan (GAG) layer — together the blood–urine barrier.
Spot the umbrella cells and you have identified urothelium. It changes apparent thickness with filling, so always judge it against how distended the organ was.
The Ureter
🔬 Image slot — ureter cross-section — star-shaped urothelial lumen, muscularis, adventitia
LayerFeatures
MucosaUrothelium + lamina propria (no muscularis mucosae) thrown into folds → a star-shaped lumen (the hallmark low-power clue)
MuscularisInner longitudinal + outer circular smooth muscle (the opposite arrangement to gut); a third outer longitudinal layer appears in the lower third
AdventitiaFibroelastic CT anchoring the retroperitoneal ureter
Muscle drives peristalsis that propels urine. Three anatomical constrictions — the pelviureteric junction, pelvic brim (iliac vessels), and vesicoureteric junction — are where stones lodge. The oblique vesicoureteric junction is an anti-reflux valve.
The Bladder
🔬 Image slot — bladder wall — urothelium, lamina propria and the interwoven detrusor smooth muscle
  • Mucosa — urothelium (up to ~6 layers when relaxed) on a vascular lamina propria; folds (rugae) that flatten on filling.
  • Muscularis = detrusor — three interwoven smooth-muscle layers (not the neat separate layers of gut); contracts to void.
  • Trigone — a smooth, rugae-free triangle (between the two ureteric orifices & the urethra). Origin debated: traditionally taught as mesonephric-duct (mesodermal), but modern lineage-tracing suggests it is largely endodermal like the rest of the bladder.
  • Outer adventitia, with serosa (peritoneum) over the superior surface/dome only.
Neural control of micturition
Parasympathetic (pelvic, S2–4, M3) → contracts detrusor (voiding)
Sympathetic (hypogastric, T11–L2) → β₃ relaxes detrusor, α₁ contracts internal sphincter (storage)
Somatic (pudendal, S2–4) → voluntary external urethral sphincter
Pontine micturition centre (Barrington) coordinates voiding; the spinal reflex (S2–4) is normally under suprapontine inhibition — cord injury → detrusor-sphincter dyssynergia.
Ureter vs Bladder — Quick Contrast
Ureter
  • Star-shaped lumen
  • Thin urothelium (2–3 layers)
  • Discrete inner longitudinal / outer circular muscle
Bladder
  • Broad wall, rugae when empty
  • Thicker urothelium (up to ~6 layers)
  • Interwoven detrusor muscle bundles
Stains & Markers
  • H&E — umbrella cells, star-shaped ureteric lumen, detrusor bundles.
  • Uroplakin & CK7 / CK20 / GATA3 / p63 (IHC) — confirm urothelial differentiation (urothelial carcinoma).
  • Cytology of voided urine — screens for high-grade urothelial carcinoma.
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Urothelial (transitional cell) carcinoma
Commonest bladder cancer; painless haematuria; risk: smoking, aromatic amines (2-naphthylamine, benzidine), cyclophosphamide. Papillary (Ta/T1) vs flat CIS; key split = non-muscle-invasive (TURBT/BCG) vs muscle-invasive ≥T2 (cystectomy).
Schistosomiasis
S. haematobium → chronic inflammation → squamous metaplasia → squamous cell carcinoma
Ureteric colic
Stones impact at the 3 constrictions (PUJ, pelvic brim, VUJ) → loin-to-groin pain
Vesicoureteric reflux
Incompetent oblique VUJ → reflux → recurrent pyelonephritis & reflux nephropathy (scarring)
Bladder outflow obstruction
BPH → detrusor hypertrophy & trabeculation, diverticula, retention
Cystitis / UTI
Urothelial inflammation (commonly E. coli); dysuria, frequency; can ascend to pyelonephritis. Cyclophosphamide (acrolein) → haemorrhagic cystitis (prevented by mesna).
Adenocarcinoma (urachal)
Rare; glandular metaplasia or urachal remnants at the dome; associated with bladder exstrophy.
Malakoplakia
Chronic granulomatous reaction (defective macrophage killing of E. coli) with Michaelis-Gutmann bodies (targetoid calcified inclusions).
Two bladder cancers, two settings: urothelial (transitional cell) carcinoma — smoking/dyes (most cases in the West); squamous cell carcinoma — chronic irritation, classically schistosomiasis.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Urothelium lines calyces → urethra; recognise it by the dome-shaped umbrella cells (often binucleate).
Umbrella cells + uroplakin plaques, fusiform vesicles & tight junctions = distensible, impermeable blood–urine barrier.
Urothelium changes apparent thickness with filling (5–6 layers relaxed → 2–3 flat when distended).
Ureter muscle = inner longitudinal + outer circular (opposite of gut); star-shaped lumen.
Stone sites = PUJ, pelvic brim, VUJ; the oblique VUJ is the anti-reflux valve.
Detrusor = interwoven smooth muscle; voiding = parasympathetic M3, storage = sympathetic (β₃ detrusor, α₁ sphincter), voluntary sphincter = pudendal.
Trigone is smooth & mesodermal (mesonephric-duct) in origin.
Bladder cancer: urothelial (smoking/dyes) vs squamous (schistosomiasis); painless haematuria is the red flag.
RENAL__Renal Vasculature:
Overview — A Vasculature Built for Filtering

The kidneys receive ~20–25% of the cardiac output for their size. Their circulation is unusual: two capillary beds in series bracketed by arterioles, plus the hair-pin vasa recta that protect the medullary gradient.

🔬 Image slot — renal arterial tree — renal artery to arcuate/cortical radiate arteries and the glomerular circulation
Key oddity: blood passes an afferent arteriole → glomerular capillaries → efferent arteriole → a SECOND capillary bed (peritubular or vasa recta). Two capillary beds in series bridged by the efferent arteriole — an arteriolar portal arrangement (unlike the classic venous portal systems, hepatic & hypophyseal).
The Arterial Pathway
1
Renal → segmental arterySegmental & interlobar arteries are end arteries (no anastomoses; avascular Brödel line between anterior/posterior territories)
2
Interlobar arteriesRun between pyramids (in the columns of Bertin)
3
Arcuate arteriesArch over the base of the pyramids at the corticomedullary junction
4
Cortical radiate (interlobular)Ascend through the cortex; give off afferent arterioles
5
Afferent → glomerulus → efferentFiltration bed between two arterioles
Arcuate arteries mark the corticomedullary junction — a reliable low-power landmark. Interlobar vessels sit in the columns between pyramids.
Two Capillary Beds in Series
🔬 Image slot — portal arrangement — glomerular capillaries then peritubular capillaries / vasa recta
1. Glomerular capillaries
  • Fenestrated, high pressure → filtration
  • Between afferent (in) and efferent (out) arterioles
2. Peritubular / vasa recta
  • From the efferent arteriole; low hydrostatic + high oncotic pressure (protein-free filtrate removed at the glomerulus) → reabsorption
  • Peritubular capillaries wrap cortical tubules; vasa recta descend into medulla
The high-pressure first bed filters; the low-pressure second bed reclaims what the tubules reabsorb. The efferent arteriole’s tone (set by angiotensin II) controls the pressure split between them.
Vasa Recta & Countercurrent Exchange
🔬 Image slot — vasa recta hair-pins running alongside the loops of Henle in the medulla
  • Long straight capillaries from juxtamedullary efferent arterioles; run as hair-pin loops parallel to the loops of Henle.
  • Act as a countercurrent exchanger: they passively pick up and re-deposit solute/water so they supply the medulla without washing out its osmotic gradient.
  • Carry away the water reabsorbed by the collecting duct.
  • The medulla is hypoxia-prone: countercurrent O₂ shunting in the vasa recta short-circuits the deep medulla, while the thick ascending limb has a high O₂ demand → the outer-medullary S3 tubule & TAL are hit first (ATN, papillary necrosis).
Countercurrent multiplier vs exchanger: the loop of Henle builds the gradient (multiplier); the vasa recta preserve it (passive exchanger).
Venous Return & Slide Recognition
  • Veins mirror the arteries: cortical radiate → arcuate → interlobar → renal vein (surface stellate veins too).
  • Arcuate vessels at the corticomedullary junction and interlobar vessels in the columns are the map landmarks.
  • Vasa recta in the medulla are thin-walled bundles — distinguish from thin limbs of Henle by the presence of red cells in the vasa recta.
  • At the vascular pole, spot the paired afferent & efferent arterioles (efferent is usually the smaller).
Autoregulation of Renal Blood Flow
Myogenic mechanism
  • ↑ BP stretches the afferent arteriole → reflex constriction
  • Stabilises flow instantly
Tubuloglomerular feedback
  • Macula densa senses NaCl → adenosine → afferent tone
  • Fine-tunes GFR (see JGA note)
Together these keep renal blood flow and GFR nearly constant across mean arterial pressures of ~80–180 mmHg.
Stains
  • H&E — vessel calibre & walls; vasa-recta bundles.
  • Elastic (EVG) — arterial elastic laminae; intimal fibroelastosis in hypertension.
  • PAS — hyaline arteriolosclerosis (glassy pink thickening of the afferent arteriole) in hypertension & diabetes.
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Renal artery stenosis
Atherosclerosis (ostial, older) or fibromuscular dysplasia (young women, “string of beads”) → renovascular hypertension
Renal infarction
Segmental arteries are end arteries → embolism causes a wedge-shaped infarct
Hypertensive nephrosclerosis
Hyaline arteriolosclerosis of the afferent arteriole → ischaemic glomerular loss, small granular kidney
Diabetic vascular change
Hyaline arteriolosclerosis of both afferent AND efferent arterioles (characteristic)
Acute tubular necrosis / papillary necrosis
The oxygen-poor medulla (vasa recta supply) is hit first by ischaemia
Renal vein thrombosis
Associated with nephrotic syndrome (esp. membranous); flank pain, worsening proteinuria
Thrombotic microangiopathy
HUS/TTP → fibrin thrombi in glomerular capillaries & arterioles; schistocytes, AKI
Cholesterol atheroembolism
Post-angiography → cholesterol clefts in arcuate/interlobular arteries → AKI
Malignant hypertension
Onion-skin hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis + arteriolar fibrinoid necrosis → “flea-bitten” petechial kidney, AKI.
Polyarteritis nodosa
Medium-vessel (interlobar/arcuate) necrotising vasculitis; transmural fibrinoid necrosis + microaneurysms (rosary); spares glomeruli, ANCA-neg, HBV-linked.
Left renal vein / nutcracker
Longer left renal vein crosses anterior to the aorta (aorto-SMA angle), receiving left gonadal & adrenal veins; compression → left varicocele, flank pain, haematuria.
Scleroderma renal crisis
Onion-skin intimal proliferation + fibrinoid necrosis + TMA of interlobular arteries → malignant HTN & AKI; treated with ACE inhibitors.
Two arteriolosclerosis clues: afferent-only hyaline change → think hypertension; afferent + efferent hyaline change → think diabetes.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Arterial order: renal → segmental → interlobar → arcuate → cortical radiate (interlobular) → afferent → glomerulus → efferent.
Two capillary beds in series (glomerular then peritubular/vasa recta) — a portal arrangement.
Arcuate arteries arch at the corticomedullary junction — the low-power landmark.
Vasa recta = countercurrent exchanger preserving the medullary gradient; loop of Henle = multiplier that builds it.
Segmental arteries are end arteries → occlusion causes infarction.
Autoregulation = myogenic + tubuloglomerular feedback (RBF/GFR constant ~80–180 mmHg).
Medulla is hypoxia-prone (vasa recta) → first hit in ATN & papillary necrosis.
Hyaline arteriolosclerosis: afferent-only = hypertension; afferent + efferent = diabetes.
